steps.why: Because both end values are 0, the chord slope is 0 and the mean value equation becomes f′(c) = 0 — the same equation Rolle's theorem gives for this function. Saying so shows the examiner you know why the two theorems give the same equation here.
common_mistakes: Taking sin 2π as 1 instead of 0, which makes the chord slope −1/π.
Writing only the value of c and leaving the two conditions unstated.

steps.label: Solve f′(c) = 0 for c
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Turn cos 2c into 2cos²c − 1 so the equation becomes a quadratic in cos c. Both roots of that quadratic lie between −1 and 1, so both give a usable c.
steps.memory_tip: When an equation mixes cos x with cos 2x, replace cos 2x by 2cos²x − 1 and it becomes a quadratic in cos x.

steps.why: The theorem asks for at least one c, and here the quadratic gives two. Both are inside (0, π), so either one is a complete answer; naming both shows the equation was solved rather than guessed.
common_mistakes: Differentiating sin 2x as cos 2x and losing the factor 2.
Using cos 2c = 1 − 2sin²c, which leaves both sin c and cos c in the equation.
Rejecting the negative root, which is valid because c may lie past π/2.

insider_note: f(0) and f(π) are both 0, so the average slope is 0 and this reduces to the Rolle case. Solve f′(c) = 0 as a quadratic in cos c.
